g3_extraction_pilot.verdict: FAIL as specified; PASS at 512-token chunks
g3_extraction_pilot.cause: decode-bound on extraction payload size, not model speed. One 1024-token chunk emits 4,044 output tokens at ~21 tok/s.

superlinearity_finding.status: REFUTED by a 10-pair probe. The n=1 measurement had the sign wrong.
superlinearity_finding.original_claim: Halving the chunk cuts total index time 26% AND passes the latency gate — both, not a trade. Extrapolated from ONE chunk.
superlinearity_finding.corrected_conclusion: Splitting is MORE expensive and MORE thorough, not cheaper and worse. 512x2 costs 1.33x the wall clock of 1024 and emits 1.38x the tokens, while finding 37% more entities and 30% more relationships. The trade is cost against recall, in the opposite direction to the one claimed.
superlinearity_finding.severance_claim_also_wrong: Only 39 of 133 relationships lost by splitting (29%) were provably severed by the boundary. The other 71% is extractor non-determinism across a changed context window, not a structural cost of chunking.
superlinearity_finding.corroboration: Independently consistent with the chunking workflow's measured cost exponent k=1.43 (total index cost scales as T*s^(k-1)), which also implies smaller chunks cost more in total. Their 256-token projection rises to ~24 h for the same reason.
superlinearity_finding.lesson: One chunk was an outlier with an unusually verbose whole-chunk extraction. A single measurement was used to argue for restructuring the study.

g3_extraction_pilot.open_decision: 512-token chunking is a study-wide change, not a graph-only one: the fairness contract requires identical chunking across all arms.
g3_extraction_pilot.script_bug_found: no num_predict cap in the pilot, so a runaway extraction blocked past the 600s client timeout. Cap added.

integrity.method: every pySBD sentence of every article asserted present in that article's chunks; counts checked against the source

e1_chunker.bug_found_and_fixed: BPE merges across sentence joins, so a joined chunk can tokenize LONGER than the sum of its sentences. 4 of 1,213 chunks exceeded a 600 budget by up to 3 tokens. The packer now re-counts the real joined string and carries the overflow sentences into the next chunk rather than dropping them.

vs_research_projection.note: measured is ~7-9% higher; the paragraph-boundary preference flushes early on news text, which averages 46.6 paragraphs per article. Fill is 0.831, not the projected 0.917.

baseline_naive_char_scheme.source: measured by the chunking research on the pre-existing scheme

power_control.why: 0.00% at both budgets was too clean to accept. A severance test that cannot detect severance would report 0% for a broken chunker too, so the detector was run against schemes known to sever.
power_control.conclusion: The detector has power: severance rises monotonically as chunks shrink. It reports 0% for the overlapped naive scheme because 512 chars of overlap recovers spans whose median length is 185 chars.
power_control.the_finding: Sentence alignment achieves at ZERO overlap what the naive scheme needs 512 chars of overlap to achieve: 0.00% evidence severance. Overlap costs ~12.5% more chunks and, for the graph arm, ~20% more LLM calls plus duplicate entities. Sentence alignment costs nothing at index time.
power_control.vs_prediction: Research predicted 0.5-2% residual from 6 multi-sentence gold spans and pySBD boundary error. Measured 0.00% on 4,243 spans. MultiHop-RAG's `fact` fields appear to be sentence-aligned by construction. Note the span counts differ from the research's 981 — this counts every (query, evidence) pair, not unique spans.

headline.e0_verdict: FAIL on truncation, PASS on thinking. 0 of 189 calls emitted thinking tokens, so `think:false` works and the cost model is not measuring reasoning. But 9 of 189 (4.8%) hit the 8,000-token cap and returned unparseable JSON. Truncation is a standing failure mode of local graph extraction at any fixed budget, not a nuisance to raise the cap past.
headline.cost_verdict: Smaller chunks cost MORE, now bounded. 600-chunking takes 1.328x the wall clock (95% CI 1.164-1.498) and emits 1.353x the tokens (CI 1.189-1.523) of 1200-chunking on the same articles. Both CIs exclude 1.0. This closes the superlinearity claim made from n=1, which had the sign inverted.

edge_verdict.claim: Overlap, the standard mitigation, addresses only 4% of the edges that chunking costs you.
edge_verdict.why_it_matters: Boundary severance is what overlap and gleanings are designed to fix, and it is 4% of the problem. 68% is the model declining to state a relation whose BOTH endpoints sat inside a single 600-token chunk it was shown. Extraction is deterministic here (same input, byte-identical output, verified 3x), so this is context-dependence, not sampling noise, and no overlap setting recovers it.
edge_verdict.caveat: 28.3% unclassified: one or both endpoints could not be located in any 600-chunk by substring match, usually an entity-name variant. Reported rather than reallocated.
edge_verdict.counterweight: 600-chunking is not strictly worse. It found 755 edges the 1200 chunking missed and 25% more entities (1,024 vs 821). The trade is cost and coherence against recall.

headline.verdict: Hits@10 is SATURATED on this subset and cannot discriminate. All six configurations land between 96.45% and 97.04% — a 0.59-point spread across two chunk sizes and three header variants. The metric is measuring the corpus, not the retriever.
headline.cause: 253 articles produce 694-1,214 chunks. Retrieving 10 of them is 0.8-1.4% of the corpus, and the queries were written from those very articles. Any competent embedder clears it.
headline.consequence_for_the_study: The pre-registered headline — that chunk size moves the primary metric more than architecture does — CANNOT be tested with Hits@10 on this subset. Measured chunk-size effect on the dense arm is 0.20-0.59 points, against the 16.1 points the research projected for the hybrid arm across 150-1200. Either the projection does not transfer to dense retrieval, or the ceiling is hiding it. Both require a harder primary metric before Stage 1.
options_in_preference_order: Harder metric: strict all-evidence-retrieved (every gold doc for a query in top-k), or Hits@1. MRR@10 already shows 4x the spread of Hits@10 (0.031 vs 0.0059).
Full 609-article corpus rather than the tech+business subset — 2.4x the distractors, and it costs graph index hours proportionally.

title_prepend_does_not_help_dense.note: The research measured +1.0 for title and +3.5 for title+source on BM25. Neither transfers to dense retrieval: BM25 wins by matching the literal outlet string, and an embedding gets no comparable windfall. The outlet-name leakage is therefore an arm-asymmetric BM25 artifact specifically, which strengthens the case for reporting the stripped configuration as primary.

by_question_type_600_title.note: comparison is the hardest stratum by 3 points even at the ceiling.
